prompt.context: A cable TV company from Canada, World View, had recently entered the US market in the northeast to expand its market share. World View saw this move as an opportunity to capture a large part of the US market (4MM consumers) in a market with very little competition.
prompt.question: However, in the last couple of years, much to the surprise of management, World View has been unable to make a profit. You have been hired to figure out why and advise them on their next move.

clarifying_info.q: Did World View incur additional costs per customer on average in the new market?
clarifying_info.a: No. Based on the potential number of subscribers, they have instituted the same system that was in place. Costs associated with cable wire, debt, maintenance costs, etc. are all proportionally the same.

clarifying_info.q: How many of the 4MM potential customers are signed up?
Are other cable companies capturing the remaining market?
clarifying_info.a: No, competition is not an issue. Those that have not been acquired as customers simply do not have cable.

clarifying_info.q: How is the consumer in the northeast US different from the Canadian consumer with respect to viewing behavior?
clarifying_info.a: The Canadian consumer does not rely much on local stations for watching TV; cable is a major source of entertainment and news coverage. In the northeast US, consumers tend to shy away from paying $40 a month and settle for watching local stations.

clarifying_info.q: Does the new market have a lower income level?
How many local stations are there and do they meet most consumer needs?
clarifying_info.a: There are about 16 local stations with coverage over the entire northeast. They provide programming that consumers want. The average consumer in the northeast watches regular TV more than cable compared with the Canadian consumer.

clarifying_info.q: Do local stations have good reception and how much do they charge?
clarifying_info.a: They have very good reception and are part of basic TV, so they are free.

clarifying_info.q: Is World View providing programming that local stations are not?
clarifying_info.a: Some, but consumers don't seem interested. They don't feel it's worth $40.

framework: Use the profitability framework: analyze both the revenue side and the cost side
On the revenue side: assess number of subscribers, pricing, and willingness to pay
On the cost side: assess whether costs per customer differ from Canada
Analyze competitive landscape — not just cable competitors but also substitutes (local/free TV)
Examine differences in consumer behavior and income between Canada and the northeast US

questions.prompt: Are costs higher in the new market compared to Canada?
questions.guidance: Costs are proportionally the same — same infrastructure model applied. Cost side is not the driver of the profitability problem.

questions.prompt: What is the revenue shortfall? How many subscribers are captured?
questions.guidance: Only 2.1MM out of 4MM potential customers have subscribed (52.5% penetration). The remaining ~1.9MM simply don't have cable — so the gap is a demand problem, not a competition problem.

math.setup: Potential customers = 4MM; Actual subscribers = 2.1MM; Penetration rate = 2.1/4.0
math.answer: ~1.9MM consumers are unreached; penetration is only ~52.5%

questions.prompt: Why are consumers unwilling to pay $40/month for cable?
questions.guidance: Northeast US consumers have ~20% lower income than Canadian consumers AND have access to 16 free local stations with good reception that meet most of their entertainment/news needs. Cable is therefore not seen as worth the incremental $40.

brainstorming.prompt: What strategies could World View pursue to improve profitability in the northeast US?

categories.name: Product/Offering
ideas: Offer a smaller, cheaper channel package targeting consumers who want only a few cable channels
Add differentiated content (sports, premium, niche) that free local stations cannot replicate
Bundle internet or phone services to increase perceived value

categories.name: Pricing
ideas: Lower the monthly price below $40 to narrow the gap vs. free local TV
Introduce tiered pricing (basic cable vs. premium)
Offer promotional introductory rates to acquire subscribers

categories.name: Geographic Focus
ideas: Scale back operations to a specific high-income region of the northeast where WTP is higher
Exit lower-density or lower-income sub-markets to cut losses

categories.name: Consumer Education & Marketing
ideas: Educate consumers on unique content and value not available on free local stations
Partner with local community organizations to raise brand awareness

categories.name: Strategic Exit
ideas: If none of the above strategies improve profitability, exit the northeast US market entirely

recommendation: World View is unprofitable in the northeast US primarily because of a demand/willingness-to-pay problem, not a cost problem: only 2.1MM of 4MM potential customers subscribe, and the remainder choose 16 free local stations with good reception instead of paying $40/month for cable

The northeast US consumer has ~20% lower income than the Canadian consumer and has strong free-TV alternatives that meet most viewing needs — the value proposition of cable at $40/month does not translate from Canada to this market
risks: Lowering price may erode margins further without sufficiently growing subscriber volume
A smaller package offering may cannibalize existing $40/month subscriber revenue
Continued operation in a structurally unattractive market burns capital while management attention is diverted
next_steps: Test a lower-priced or smaller package in a pilot region to measure price elasticity and demand response
Evaluate whether any content differentiation (e.g., sports, news) can command a premium vs. free local TV
If pilot results are negative, develop an exit plan and redeploy capital to markets with stronger cable demand
